title: Read the scanner's footprints
briefing: The dropper in `tmp/.x` got onto the box somehow. Web servers are the usual front door, and a scanner leaves a trail: hundreds of requests in a few minutes, all with the same user agent.
Count how loud the scanner was. Rotated logs count too, even the compressed one nobody remembers to read.

lesson.p: `grep PATTERN FILE...` prints every line that contains a match. Plain patterns are basic regular expressions (BRE); `-E` switches to extended syntax, so `+ ? | ( )` work without backslashes. Quote the pattern so the shell leaves it alone.

flags: invert: print the lines that do NOT match
print a count of matching lines instead of the lines; with several files you get one count per file
print only the matched text, one match per line
search every file under a directory
print only the names of files that contain a match
leave the file name off each line when several files are searched
also print N lines after / before / around each match
the same flags, but it decompresses `.gz` files first; files that are not compressed are read as they are. One exception: GNU zgrep rejects `-r` ("option not supported")

lesson.note: `grep` on a `.gz` file searches the compressed bytes, so it almost never matches and prints nothing. No error, no warning. Use `zgrep`, or `zcat -f FILES | grep`. `zcat -f` passes uncompressed files through untouched.
`grep -c` counts lines, not matches. A line with the pattern twice counts once. To count every match, use `grep -o PATTERN | wc -l`.

stages.why: Quoted because of the space: without quotes the shell would hand grep two arguments, and `password` would be taken as a file name.
Print how many lines matched instead of the lines themselves.
`-o` prints only the match: a run of digits and dots at the start of the line, which is the client IP in Apache's combined format.
`-v` drops the known-good 192.0.2.x clients. The dots are escaped because an unescaped `.` matches any character.

examples.title: Context around a match

stages.why: A password login that succeeded. Password logins are worth a second look on a host that should use keys.
Also print one line before each match. Here that line is a failed password for the same user from the same port: a typo, then success.

examples.output:
Mar 13 09:20:44 web-01 sshd[2260]: Failed password for ops_bob from 198.51.100.22 port 51544 ssh2
Mar 13 09:20:51 web-01 sshd[2260]: Accepted password for ops_bob from 198.51.100.22 port 51544 ssh2

stages.why: `-r` walks the directory; `-l` prints each matching file once instead of every matching line.
`-r` lists files in directory order, which varies; sorting makes it stable.

examples.title: grep is blind inside .gz
examples.command: gzip -c training/web.log > /tmp/web.log.gz; grep -c curl /tmp/web.log.gz; zgrep -c curl /tmp/web.log.gz

stages.why: Make a compressed copy, the way logrotate does with `compress`. `-c` writes to stdout and leaves the original alone.
Searches the compressed bytes: 0 matches, and no hint that anything is wrong.
Decompresses first and finds every curl request.

challenge.question: How many requests in the web server's access logs carry the Nikto scanner's user agent? Count across every file in var/log/httpd whose name starts with access_log, including the compressed rotation. Match the word nikto in any case.

hints: Find the scanner's lines first: `grep -i nikto` on one log. Then make sure every access_log file is searched, the `.gz` one included.

`zgrep` reads compressed and plain files alike. `-i` ignores case, `-h` drops the file names so the lines can be piped, and `wc -l` counts them. `grep -c` on several files gives one count per file, which you would have to add up.

why: Plain `grep -ic nikto var/log/httpd/access_log*` finds 60 and silently skips the compressed file. The one line it misses is the scanner's first visit, two days before the burst: the earliest sighting of the attacker on this host. You will need it for the final report.

On RHEL, logrotate compresses old logs when `compress` is set in `/etc/logrotate.conf` or a drop-in under `/etc/logrotate.d/`. During triage, start with `zgrep` or `zcat -f` across the whole rotation set. A plain `grep` reads only the logs that happen to be uncompressed.

The glob `access_log*` stops at the access logs. `var/log/httpd/old_access.txt` is a gzip copy of `access_log.2.gz` under a misleading name, so `zcat -f var/log/httpd/*` over the whole directory would count the first visit twice. Check what a file really is with `file` before you trust its name.
